job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in Birmingham with my parents and my grandmother, in the house above my dad's garage, where he does car inspections. I get up at seven, help my dad open the shop, and spend the rest of the morning on applications to big manufacturers. Afternoons I tinker with an old gearbox in the workshop, because I like to keep my hands working. I graduated from mechanical engineering in Manchester seven months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the degree and what you did in it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was a test rig for bus gearboxes, built with a bus maker, and it got a first. I did two summer placements at a car parts supplier, where I mostly checked drawings and ran tests. I'm looking for a proper graduate scheme at a big, stable firm, and I've applied to about forty. I'd rather wait for the right one than take a job I'd leave in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. Every few years there's a new buzzword, and then things carry on. At the supplier they bought some software that was meant to change everything, and in the end the team still did the drawing checks by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel steady. A plateau is a world I understand, where a good degree and a good reference should work. The only thing bothering me is that it's taking so long, and my dad keeps asking when I start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to the big firms, the three bus and car makers near Birmingham and the rail supplier. I'd ask the bus maker's engineer who supervised my project to put in a word. I'd keep helping at the garage on weekdays, and I wouldn't touch my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. It feels like waiting for a train you know is coming but hasn't been announced. I'm not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the parts supplier tell you about how often their work changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you think you're being too picky?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've waited seven months for the right one. What is that costing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My cousin took the first job he found, and he's already bored. I don't want to repeat that. But I also know my dad worries, and I'd say the honest answer is that I'm picky, and I can afford it for now.

say: I'd say that's what I expected, because every few years there's a new **buzzword** and things carry on.
I'd tell friends a good degree should still **work**.
think: I feel **steady**: a plateau is a world I understand.
The only worry is how long the **waiting** takes.
do: Apply to the **big firms** near Birmingham, including the bus makers and the rail supplier.
Ask my project supervisor at the bus maker to put in a **word**.
Keep helping at the **garage** and leave savings alone.
feel: **Restless** but not frightened, like waiting for an unannounced train.
S0.quote: My cousin took the first job he found, and he's already bored. I don't want to repeat that.
fieldNote: He is **choosy** by design, and savings let him be.
His father's quiet pressure adds a **worry** that AI doesn't cause.
He trusts big firms to stay **stable**.

steps.text: Apply to three Birmingham bus and rail makers each week
Ask the bus maker supervisor to recommend me internally
Hold out for a graduate scheme at a stable manufacturer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise. Software will take the report writing and some drawing checks, but a gearbox still has to be built and tested by people who know steel. I wouldn't panic, and I'd tell friends to focus on skills that need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm more worried than I let on. The graduate schemes that I'm waiting for might shrink, because big firms love to save on junior hiring. If the drawing checks and reports are done by software, the entry jobs I'd have done in my first year are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to smaller firms and also to test engineer roles, which still need someone on the shop floor. I'd ask the bus maker about their apprenticeship-style graduate route. And I'd start putting aside more of my savings, because waiting could last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of knot in the stomach. It isn't sleeplessness, just a feeling that the rules are changing while I stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work at the parts supplier would software take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a look at one, grudgingly. I never used them, because I never saw the need. But if that's what the supplier uses to check drawings, I'd better understand it. I'd try it on a past project, and see if it finds my mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI tool, given this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sorry, I was too fixed on the big firms. I'd tell my dad that I'll take a test engineer job even if the name is smaller, as long as it's real work. He'd say that's sensible, and he'd be right.

say: I'd say it's a lot of **noise**, because a gearbox still has to be built and tested by people who know steel.
I'd tell friends to focus on skills that need **hands**.
think: I'm more **worried** than I let on, since graduate schemes may shrink.
The entry jobs I'd have done in my **first year** could be done by software.
do: Widen my search to **smaller firms** and test engineer roles.
Ask the bus maker about their **apprenticeship-style** graduate route.
Put aside more **savings**, because waiting could last longer.
feel: A **knot** in the stomach: the rules are changing while I stand still.
S1.quote: The graduate schemes that I'm waiting for might shrink, because big firms love to save on junior hiring.
fieldNote: He openly says he's more worried than his public line.
The shift to **smaller firms** is a real change of mind.

steps.text: Apply to smaller test engineer roles in the Midlands
Move another 200 pounds a month into savings
Try an AI drawing checker on my gearbox project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster in the making. Nobody is ready, not the government, not the firms, not families. I'd say the state has to step in with income support, and I'd stay out of the shouting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. The thinking part of engineering would be done by software, and the physical part would follow in three years. My dad's garage isn't safe either, because robots can inspect cars. I think I'd be the one who has to keep the house going, since my father's trade would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any real job in a factory or lab, right away, because waiting for the perfect scheme would be silly. I'd cut my spending to what I need, and put every bit of pay into savings. I'd also ask my uncle, who works at a rail depot, about hands-on jobs there. And I'd learn to use the AI tools, grudgingly, because refusing would be pride, not sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor falling away. I'd be angry at myself for waiting so long for the perfect scheme. I'd be afraid for my parents and my grandmother, who rely on the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years for thinking AI, robots after that. What happens to your gearbox work and your garage job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad first, in the garage, over a cup of tea. I'd say we need to plan, together, for what happens to the business. He'd say it will be fine, and I'd say that isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my uncle at the rail depot too. He's a practical man, and I'd ask what he sees on the shop floor. If he says robots aren't close, I'd believe him more than a news article.

say: I'd say this is a **disaster** in the making and the state must step in with income support.
I'd stay out of the shouting **online**.
think: Software takes the **thinking** side and robots follow, so my father's garage is not safe either.
I might have to **keep** the house going.
do: Take any real **factory** or lab job right away.
Cut spending to needs and put every bit of pay into **savings**.
Ask my uncle about hands-on jobs at the **rail depot**.
feel: The **floor falling away**, with anger at myself for waiting.
S2.quote: My dad's garage isn't safe either, because robots can inspect cars.
fieldNote: His fear includes his father's **garage** and his grandmother.
He trusts his uncle's shop-floor view over the news, which fits his cautious character.

steps.text: Take the first real factory or lab job offered in the Midlands
Cut spending to rent share, food and travel
Put every pay cheque above 800 pounds into savings
Learn an AI tool for drawing checks, reluctantly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for firms to adjust and for governments to act, if they begin soon. I'd tell friends to be practical, to get a real job and learn something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel anxious but not alarmed. I could land a first job and put in three years, and that experience is worth something even if the thinking part is automated. Robots reach hands-on work three years after, so I'd have a bit of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a manufacturing job I can learn from, maybe at the rail supplier. I'd study for my chartered engineer status, since it's a title that is harder for software to copy. I'd save a third of my pay and I'd keep helping at the garage in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than two years. It feels like a long hill, where you know it's steep but there's a path. I'd still have some bad nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my dad: let's change the garage a little, add electric car checks. In five years that skill is worth money. I'd help him do it, since I understand the technical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change what you would say to your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garage could be a base. If I have a decent job and he adapts, we're both better placed. It's the first time I'd feel part of his business, not just a helper.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for firms to adjust if they begin **soon**.
I'd tell friends to get a real job and learn something that **lasts**.
think: I'd feel **anxious** but not alarmed, because three years of experience still counts.
Robots reach **hands-on work** three years later, so I'd have room.

Save a third of my pay and keep helping at the **garage**.

S3.quote: I'd study for my chartered engineer status, since it's a title that is harder for software to copy.
fieldNote: Time lets him pick a **credential** he thinks software can't copy.

Still anxious, but with a clear route.

steps.text: Take a manufacturing job at the rail supplier and learn the work
Start the chartered engineer route with a professional body
Save a third of every pay cheque
Help my dad add electric car checks to the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and the world will find a way. Our grandparents lived through bigger changes. I'd tell friends to stay calm and keep to their trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be mostly calm. I'd have time to build a career, buy a house, maybe start a family. The change will come, but I'd have a decade to learn what to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still wait a few more months for the right scheme, but not forever. I'd become a chartered engineer, specialise in test and validation, and watch what the car makers do. I'd buy a small house in my thirties, near my parents, and keep the habit of saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. It feels a bit like looking at a map of a long trip: far but doable. I wouldn't lose sleep, though I'd keep one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what are you willing to do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set a deadline. If there's no offer in three more months I'd take a good smaller firm. In a ten-year picture, my first job matters less than my second or third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still wait for a graduate scheme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, a bit. But with ten years, I'd say it's no longer about being safe. It's about being useful, and I'd want to be useful in a place I can see with my own eyes.

say: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and the world will find a **way**.
I'd tell friends to stay calm and keep to their **trade**.
think: I'd be mostly **calm**, with time to build a career and maybe a family.
The change will come, but I'd have a **decade** to learn what to do.

feel: **Fine**, like looking at a map of a long trip.
S4.quote: In a ten-year picture, my first job matters less than my second or third.
fieldNote: He sets a self-made **deadline**, a sign of resistance softening.

steps.text: Set a three-month deadline for a graduate scheme offer
Specialise in test and validation and become chartered
Save for a small house near my parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It leaves no room to build anything, and my dad's garage would be hit as well. What would help is real jobs on offer, honest talk from firms and a public plan for ordinary families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I've been stubborn, and I know it. I wanted the perfect firm, and the world might not wait. I'd tell other graduates to be a bit less proud than I was.

headlineQuote: I've been stubborn, and I know it. I wanted the perfect firm, and the world might not wait.
portrait: Femi is **23**, a mechanical engineering graduate in Birmingham, living above his father's car-inspection garage.
He is choosy about big, **stable** firms and has avoided AI tools so far.
His public line is calm, but private worries about his family's **garage** grow with each scenario.
He moves from pride to **practicality** as the warning time shortens.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, which leaves no time and also hits his father's garage.
whatWouldHelp: Real **jobs** on offer, honest talk from firms and a public plan for ordinary families.
